sources.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models

omissions: Figure images were not included in the supplied text extraction. Captions and embedded textual examples were read, but no PDF figures were visually inspected and no curve values were extracted.
No explicit arXiv revision number was supplied. Title and authors match the catalog; the reviewed source is identified by the supplied provenance and SHA-256.
Figure images are not included in the text extraction; source captions and numerical tables are present.
tablesReviewed: Model sizes, architectures, and optimization hyper-parameters (tab:architecture)
Zero-shot performance on Common Sense Reasoning tasks (tab:commonsense)
Model performance on quantitative reasoning datasets (tab:math)
Carbon footprint of training different models in the same data center (tab:cf)

synopsis: LLaMA investigates how much language-task performance smaller models can obtain through substantially longer pretraining. It combines a documented text mixture, established transformer modifications and efficient distributed training to produce models spanning 7B–65B parameters. The authors emphasize inference affordability and publicly available training sources. [E01–E07] Reader assessment: the results establish a strong empirical language-model recipe, with strengths in question answering and competitive code generation, but uneven performance across knowledge and mathematical tasks. They do not isolate the contribution of each architectural choice or demonstrate embodied prediction and control. [E09–E16]

problem.text: Training-compute-optimal scaling does not necessarily minimize the cost of repeatedly serving a model. The authors therefore seek strong performance at different model sizes by spending more training tokens on smaller networks, while avoiding reliance on inaccessible training corpora.

contributions.text: A family of causal language models trained on a disclosed mixture of web text, code, books, scientific articles and question-answer discussions, with model configurations and optimization settings reported.
An implementation combining memory-efficient attention, selective activation storage, custom backward computation and distributed parallelism to make long pretraining practical.

The principal contribution is the combined training recipe and its empirical performance. RMSNorm, SwiGLU and rotary embeddings are adopted from earlier work; their individual benefits are not isolated experimentally here.

inputs: Pretraining: tokenized text and code sampled from the disclosed corpus mixture. [E03, E04]
Evaluation: a textual task description or question, optionally demonstrations, passages, candidate answers or a program specification. [E08, E10, E13, E15]
outputs: Conditional token predictions used to generate answers, prose or Python programs, or to score candidate completions. [E08, E15]
Reader assessment: the described outputs do not include a physical action representation or an environment-state prediction interface. [E05, E08]

steps.name: Construct and filter the training mixture
steps.detail: Sampling proportions are CommonCrawl 67%, C4 15%, GitHub 4.5%, Wikipedia 4.5%, books 4.5%, arXiv 2.5% and Stack Exchange 2%. CommonCrawl undergoes line deduplication, language and quality filtering, plus a Wikipedia-reference classifier. GitHub filtering retains Apache, BSD and MIT projects and removes exact duplicate files. Books are deduplicated by content overlap; arXiv processing removes bibliographies and expands macros.

steps.name: Convert documents into token sequences
steps.detail: SentencePiece implements byte-pair encoding. Numbers are split into individual digits, and unknown UTF-8 characters fall back to bytes. The mixture includes multilingual Wikipedia, although the main web component is filtered for English.

steps.name: Predict tokens with a causal transformer
steps.detail: Causal attention restricts prediction to preceding context. Each transformer sublayer receives RMS-normalized inputs; feed-forward computation uses SwiGLU with intermediate dimension (2/3) × 4d, where d is the model dimension. Rotary positional embeddings replace absolute positional embeddings at every layer.

steps.name: Adapt the prediction interface to each task
steps.detail: Evaluation either generates a continuation or ranks candidate completions. Few-shot examples enter the prompt rather than constituting a new training stage. The separate LLaMA-I experiment instead changes model weights through instruction finetuning.

training.text: The reported parameter counts are 6.7B, 13.0B, 32.5B and 65.2B, corresponding to the named 7B, 13B, 33B and 65B models. Their dimension/head/layer configurations are respectively 4096/32/32, 5120/40/40, 6656/52/60 and 8192/64/80. Smaller models consume 1.0T tokens; larger models consume 1.4T. Every configuration in the table uses a 4M-token batch.

Causal language modeling uses AdamW with beta values 0.9 and 0.95, weight decay 0.1, gradient clipping 1.0 and 2,000 warmup steps. Peak learning rates are 3.0e-4 for the smaller models and 1.5e-4 for the larger models; cosine decay ends at 10% of the peak. The paper does not provide an explicit loss equation.

The authors report approximately 380 tokens/second/GPU for the 65B model on 2,048 A100 GPUs with 80GB memory, yielding approximately 21 days for its training run. These are reported training-throughput figures, not measured serving latency.

LLaMA-I comes from a single instruction-finetuning experiment using the cited instruction dataset and protocol. The supplied paper does not specify a self-contained finetuning schedule or frozen-module configuration.

inference.text: Most multiple-choice tasks rank completions using likelihood normalized by completion character count. BoolQ and OpenBookQA instead use the likelihood ratio below.

Closed-book QA uses greedy decoding without supporting documents. Answers terminate at the first newline, final dot or comma, then undergo lowercasing and removal of articles, punctuation and duplicate whitespace before exact-match scoring.

Mathematical majority voting selects an answer from multiple generated samples. Code pass@1 uses sampling temperature 0.1, whereas pass@100 and pass@80 use 0.8. These decoding protocols change evaluation-time computation and should not be conflated.

equations.explanation: For BoolQ and OpenBookQA, the model selects the completion with the largest ratio. The denominator adjusts for the completion's likelihood under a generic answer prefix. This is an evaluation scoring rule, not a training objective.

results.setting: Zero-shot; benchmark split is not explicitly named in the supplied text.
results.interpretation: Reader analysis: this supports competitive performance at substantially smaller parameter count on this task, without establishing an inference-speed ratio.

results.setting: 64-shot; open-domain QA test split containing 3,610 questions; greedy decoding.
results.interpretation: Reader analysis: the advantage over PaLM is small, and the table supplies no uncertainty estimate.

results.setting: Zero-shot; filtered development set; greedy decoding.
results.interpretation: Reader analysis: this is a strong reported QA result. The appendix explicitly distinguishes this split from the unfiltered test set used by GPT-3 and PaLM.

results.setting: Zero-shot RACE-middle and RACE-high; split not explicitly identified.
results.interpretation: Reader analysis: competitiveness varies by subset; LLaMA does not lead both.

results.setting: Reported standard evaluation and majority voting with 100 samples; split and prompt shot count are not stated.
results.value: LLaMA-65B: 50.9 without majority voting; 69.7 with majority voting
results.comparison: Minerva-62B: 52.4 without majority voting; 68.5 with majority voting
results.interpretation: Reader analysis: the paper's claimed advantage over Minerva-62B holds for majority voting, not the non-voting column. Additional sampling is an inference intervention, not an architectural ablation.
Reader analysis: LLaMA ties the continued-training baseline here and trails PaLM-540B. The metric concerns generated programs passing tests, not physical execution.
Reader analysis: this supports competitive general-model code generation without code-specific finetuning; the small lead over PaLM-540B has no reported uncertainty.

results.setting: Five-shot using benchmark examples; test sets.
results.comparison: Chinchilla-70B: 67.5 in the main table; PaLM-540B: 69.3
results.interpretation: Reader analysis: the base model remains behind both comparators, qualifying the broader claim of competitiveness.

results.setting: Five-shot test evaluation after the single LLaMA-I finetuning experiment.
results.interpretation: Reader analysis: the increase is 5.5 percentage points. It demonstrates an adaptation benefit but does not isolate instruction formatting from additional supervised data.

results.setting: RealToxicityPrompts; 100,000 prompts; greedy decoding with Basic and Respectful prefixes.
results.metric: Mean automatic toxicity score, 0–1; lower is better
results.comparison: The Respectful condition scores worse than Basic for the same model.
results.interpretation: Reader analysis: a politeness instruction does not ensure less toxic output under this protocol. These scores are not percentages of toxic generations.

results.setting: TruthfulQA generation using the stated QA prompt style; specially trained API-based evaluators.
results.metric: Fraction truthful; fraction both truthful and informative
results.interpretation: Reader analysis: improvement over the reported baseline coexists with substantial remaining error; automated benchmark judgments do not establish general factual reliability.

limitations.text: The study does not isolate architectural changes or training-data composition through controlled ablations. Training-progress prose supports continued improvement, but figure images absent from the supplied text extraction prevent independent assessment of the curves. The inference-budget motivation is also not accompanied by a measured serving-latency comparison.

Baseline numbers generally come from other papers, with differences in data, training budgets and sometimes evaluation splits. Consequently, parameter-count comparisons establish empirical competitiveness rather than a controlled causal estimate of the LLaMA recipe's benefit.

Several narrative statements need qualification against the tables. Contrary to the stated BoolQ exception, LLaMA-65B scores 85.3 versus Chinchilla's 83.7. LLaMA-33B also exceeds 65B on zero-shot Natural Questions, 24.9 versus 23.8. Chinchilla's MMLU aggregate is 67.5 in the main table but 67.6 in the appendix; this report retains the explicitly identified main-table value.
The suggested explanation for weaker MMLU performance—less book and academic material—remains an untested data-composition hypothesis.

The authors acknowledge that the selected safety benchmarks cannot fully characterize model risks. They report stereotype preferences and lower WinoGender performance on occupation/pronoun gotcha cases, alongside continuing truthfulness failures.

RealToxicityPrompts comparisons are sensitive to decoding and evaluator changes. The body names PerspectiveAPI while the table caption says PerplexityAPI; the table values are legible, but the evaluator naming is internally inconsistent. Appendix generations are illustrative samples, and the simulated terminal dialogue does not demonstrate actual environment interaction.

reproduction.text: Pretraining reproduction requires reconstructing the corpus snapshots, filters, mixture sampling, tokenizer, model configurations and distributed implementation. The supplied text leaves some filtering thresholds, context length and tokenizer vocabulary size unspecified; it does specify a greater-than-90% content-overlap threshold for book deduplication. Instruction finetuning additionally depends on an externally cited protocol whose contents were not supplied.

Evaluation should preserve QA answer truncation and normalization, exact benchmark splits, completion-scoring rules, code temperatures and mathematics sample counts. The paper announces a research-model release, but no repository or weights were inspected and no experiments were reproduced in this review.

For scale planning, the paper reports 1,022,362 GPU-hours for 65B training. Its 449 MWh and 173 tCO2-equivalent estimates assume 400 W per GPU, PUE 1.1 and a shared US-average carbon intensity; these are normalized estimates, not measured location-specific emissions.

A smaller mechanism test would hold a reduced-scale version of the architecture and mixture fixed while comparing token budgets with appropriately matched learning-rate schedules. Held-out loss and downstream accuracy would test the longer-training argument; separately measured latency and memory would test its deployment rationale. Such an experiment would be a proxy study, not a full LLaMA reproduction.

reasoning.text: The recorded Foundational work / Language & VLM backbones placement is supported specifically on the language-backbone side. The architecture processes text with causal attention and produces token predictions or completion scores. It defines neither joint future-state/action prediction nor inverse dynamics, visual prediction, a robot action head or a feedback controller. Architecture, prediction paradigm and quadrant are therefore not applicable under the WAM taxonomy. The presence of one language network does not justify a WAM One Model classification.

discussionQuestions: What measured serving workload would justify the extra pretraining cost of a smaller, longer-trained model? [E02, E07]
Would a controlled increase in book and scientific data close the MMLU gap while preserving other capabilities? [E03, E16]
Why does instruction finetuning improve aggregate MMLU while some individual subjects deteriorate? [E18]
How much of the GSM8k improvement survives when models receive equal inference-time sampling budgets? [E14]

evidence.location: Title, author block and Abstract
evidence.detail: The title and author list match the supplied catalog. The abstract introduces the 7B–65B family and announces release to the research community.

evidence.location: Introduction, paragraphs on training versus inference budgets
evidence.detail: The authors motivate longer training of smaller models by inference cost and report continued improvement of a 7B model after 1T tokens.

evidence.location: Approach > Pre-training Data; dataset paragraphs and tab:dataset
evidence.detail: The section specifies corpus sources, filtering procedures, language coverage and sampling proportions; the table also gives subset epochs and storage sizes.

evidence.location: Approach > Pre-training Data, Tokenizer paragraph
evidence.detail: Tokenization uses SentencePiece BPE, individual number digits and byte fallback for unknown UTF-8 characters.

evidence.location: Approach > Architecture; tab:architecture, all model rows
evidence.detail: The architecture uses pre-normalization with RMSNorm, SwiGLU and rotary embeddings. The table provides parameter counts, dimensions, heads, layers, learning rates, batch size and training-token budgets.

evidence.location: Approach > Optimizer
evidence.detail: AdamW uses betas 0.9/0.95, weight decay 0.1, clipping 1.0, 2,000 warmup steps and cosine decay to one tenth of peak learning rate.

evidence.location: Approach > Efficient implementation
evidence.detail: The section describes causal attention, selective activation storage, custom backward computation, model/sequence parallelism and communication overlap. Reported 65B throughput is approximately 380 tokens/second/GPU on 2,048 A100-80GB GPUs, with approximately 21 days of training.

evidence.location: Main results, zero-shot/few-shot definitions and completion-scoring paragraph
evidence.detail: Tasks use generation or candidate ranking. Most candidate likelihoods are character-normalized; BoolQ and OpenBookQA use the displayed conditional-likelihood ratio.

evidence.location: Main results > Common Sense Reasoning; tab:commonsense, HellaSwag and BoolQ columns
evidence.detail: HellaSwag lists LLaMA-13B 79.2 and GPT-3 78.9. BoolQ lists LLaMA-65B 85.3 and Chinchilla 83.7, despite the prose naming BoolQ as an exception to LLaMA's advantage. Baselines are taken from corresponding papers.

evidence.location: Closed-book Question Answering; Appendix > Question Answering
evidence.detail: Natural Questions uses a 3,610-question test split; TriviaQA uses filtered development data, unlike GPT-3 and PaLM's unfiltered test evaluation. The appendix specifies greedy decoding, answer stopping rules and exact-match normalization.

evidence.location: NaturalQuestions table, tab:nqa, 0-shot and 64-shot columns
evidence.detail: At 64 shots, LLaMA-65B scores 39.9, PaLM-540B 39.6 and Chinchilla 35.5. At zero shots, LLaMA-33B scores 24.9 versus 65B's 23.8.

evidence.location: TriviaQA table, tab:tqa, 0-shot column and caption
evidence.detail: The filtered-development evaluation reports zero-shot exact match of 68.2 for LLaMA-65B and 55.4 for Chinchilla.

evidence.location: Main results > Reading Comprehension; tab:readingcomprehension
evidence.detail: Zero-shot RACE-middle/high accuracy is 67.9/51.6 for LLaMA-65B and 68.1/49.1 for PaLM-540B.

evidence.location: Main results > Mathematical reasoning; tab:math, GSM8k columns and caption
evidence.detail: LLaMA-65B scores 50.9 without voting and 69.7 with voting; Minerva-62B scores 52.4 and 68.5. Their GSM8k voting setting uses 100 samples. Minerva receives mathematical finetuning, while LLaMA does not.

evidence.location: Main results > Code generation; tab:code and decoding paragraphs
evidence.detail: HumanEval is zero-shot and MBPP three-shot. LLaMA-65B pass@1 is 23.7/37.7, PaLM-540B 26.2/36.8 and PaLM-cont-62B 23.7/31.2. LLaMA uses temperature 0.1 for pass@1 and 0.8 for the larger-k estimates.

evidence.location: Main results > Massive Multitask Language Understanding; tab:mmlu, Average column
evidence.detail: Five-shot averages are LLaMA-65B 63.4, Chinchilla 67.5 and PaLM-540B 69.3. The authors suggest limited book and academic data as a possible explanation for LLaMA's deficit.

evidence.location: Main results > Evolution of performance during training
evidence.detail: The prose reports generally improving benchmark performance, SIQA variability and weaker correspondence between WinoGrande performance and training perplexity. Referenced curve images were not included in the supplied text extraction.

evidence.location: Instruction Finetuning, tab:instruct; Appendix > MMLU, tab:mmluapp
evidence.detail: A single instruction-finetuning experiment raises aggregate MMLU from 63.4 to 68.9. The appendix identifies test-set evaluation, includes individual-domain regressions and lists Chinchilla's aggregate as 67.6 rather than the main table's 67.5.

evidence.location: Bias, Toxicity and Misinformation, opening paragraph; RealToxicityPrompts and tab:RealToxicityPrompts
evidence.detail: The authors state that benchmark coverage is incomplete. Greedy evaluation over 100k prompts gives LLaMA-65B mean toxicity 0.128 for Basic and 0.141 for Respectful. The body names PerspectiveAPI, while the caption names PerplexityAPI.

evidence.location: Bias, Toxicity and Misinformation > CrowS-Pairs and WinoGender; tab:crows and tab:winogender
evidence.detail: CrowS-Pairs measures stereotypical sentence preference. WinoGender compares pronoun-conditioned coreference performance, including gotcha cases that conflict with occupation-gender stereotypes; LLaMA-65B performs worse on those cases.

evidence.location: Bias, Toxicity and Misinformation > TruthfulQA; tab:TuthfulQA and caption
evidence.detail: API-based trained evaluators give truthful/truthful-and-informative fractions of 0.57/0.53 for LLaMA-65B and 0.28/0.25 for GPT-3-175B. The authors acknowledge continuing incorrect answers.

evidence.location: Carbon footprint; tab:cf, LLaMA-65B row and caption
evidence.detail: The table reports 1,022,362 GPU-hours, 449 MWh and 173 tCO2-equivalent. Estimates assume 400 W GPU power, PUE 1.1 and US-average intensity of 0.385 kg CO2-equivalent/kWh.

evidence.location: Appendix > Generations from LLaMA-65B and Generations from LLaMA-I
evidence.detail: The appendix supplies illustrative textual generations, including code, dialogue and a prompted simulation of terminal output; it reports no actual terminal or robot interaction for these examples.
